A small app in your Applications folder that starts Seisa and opens it in the browser, so you do not have to type anything in the terminal.

about.colors_note: The themes base their colours on traditional Japanese colours, though they are not exact copies.
about.colors_washi_intro: Washi is traditional handmade Japanese paper: warm and soft, never pure white. The status colours are darkened so that red, green and amber text stays readable on paper.
about.colors_sumi_intro: Sumi is ink, here thinned with water: night in blue-black, never pure black. The status colours are lighter so they stand out against it.
about.colors_kohaku_intro: Kōhaku means "red and white" in Japan: the pair of colours of celebrations and festivals, and also the colours of the Polish and Japanese flags, so the theme is a sign of friendship between the two countries. The background is a warm white, the red of the accent is shared by both flags, and the error red is darker so that it is not mistaken for the accent.
about.colors_brown_intro: Brown Sumi is ink again, but in its warm shade: night the colour of wet earth instead of blue-black, never pure black. Ink made from the soot of burnt oil is warmer and browner than ink made from pine soot. The accent is a muted brown-grey, so the status colours are the only bright ones.
about.col.torinoko: the colour of an eggshell: a warm, slightly yellowish cream. Named after torinoko paper, a traditional paper in that colour.
about.col.sumi: ink: the black of the ink stick used in calligraphy.
about.col.ai: indigo, the blue dyed from the indigo plant. The most "Japanese" blue.
about.col.beni: red from the pigment of the safflower, the classic red of dyes and lipstick.
about.col.matsuba: pine-needle green: deep and a little muted.
about.col.yamabuki: the golden yellow of the Kerria japonica flower.
about.col.nureba: the sheen of a wet crow's feather: a deep blue-black, not pure black. In Japan it is how the most beautiful black hair is described.
about.col.shironeri: the warm white of refined silk; it does not glare like a plain light grey.
about.col.asagi: a pale blue-green, turquoise. The name means "pale leek": the green of a leek leaf diluted with water.
about.col.shu: vermilion, the red made from cinnabar; the red of shrine gates, slightly lightened.
about.col.wakatake: young bamboo: a fresh, light green.
about.col.enji: a deep, dark red, once a dye for fabrics and lipstick; here it keeps an error apart from the brighter accent.
about.col.kurotsurubami: a brown so dark it is almost black, dyed with a decoction of acorn caps and fixed with iron. In Japan it is also the colour of mourning.
about.col.rikyushiracha: a muted, pale brown with the tone of tea. "Rikyū" in a colour name points to Sen no Rikyū, the tea master (about 1522-1591); here it is the soft brown-grey of links and buttons.
about.col.tokiha: the colour of an ibis wing: a warm, pale pink. Here a little deeper, so that an error is visible without being harsh.
about.col.byakuroku: a pale green, a pigment of Japanese painting made by grinding malachite very fine: the finer the grains, the paler the colour. Here a calm, greyish green for OK.
about.col.kikuchiba: the colour of fallen autumn leaves, known since the Heian period: a yellow-orange once dyed with gardenia and madder. Here a warm ochre for warnings.
about.limits_hint:
Assumed limits of the free plans: AbuseIPDB 5,000/day | GreyNoise 50/week | OTX 10,000/hour | Cloudflare 1,200/5 minutes.
VirusTotal, urlscan and OpenRouter report the real limits and the LLM credit when you click "Refresh limits" (one request to each service; these requests do not use up quota).
AbuseIPDB and Cloudflare take the values from the rate-limit headers of the latest requests.
GreyNoise and OTX report nothing, so Seisa counts its own requests.
WHOIS/rDNS needs no key because it uses the public, free RDAP and DNS services.
When a service answers with error 429 (limit exceeded), its row gets a "limit exceeded" badge and a full counter until the next successful answer.
about.lim_exceeded_title: The service answered with HTTP 429 (limit exceeded): {time}. The badge disappears after the next successful answer.
about.lim_state_exceeded: {service} ({scope}): the API reported the limit as used up
about.changes_hint: The 10 most recent changes from the git log of this directory (the messages are in English).
about.changes_empty: The change log is available only when Seisa runs from a git checkout.
about.name_meaning: a Japanese word meaning a thorough, detailed examination - looking at something closely.

lookup.subtitle:
Check the reputation of an IP address or a domain in several independent threat-intelligence sources at once and see one aggregate risk score.
For an IP address: VirusTotal, AlienVault OTX, Cloudflare Radar, AbuseIPDB, GreyNoise and WHOIS/rDNS.
For a domain: VirusTotal, AlienVault OTX, Cloudflare Radar, WHOIS/DNS, local heuristics.
urlscan.subtitle: Submit a live scan of a suspicious URL to urlscan.io - you get a detailed report on the page content, network traffic, detected technologies and verdict without opening the link yourself.
urlscan.url_label: URL to scan. Several addresses: separate them with a space or a new line (up to 5)
urlscan.no_uuid: urlscan.io did not return a scan identifier.
urlscan.submitted: Scan submitted - waiting for the result...
urlscan.still_running: The scan is still running after {time} - check manually
urlscan.hint.unlisted: Unlisted: the scan is hidden from the urlscan.io front page and public search, but stays visible to verified security researchers in urlscan Pro.
urlscan.hint.private: Private: the scan is visible only to your urlscan.io account - it counts against the separate private-scan quota.
urlscan.hint.public:
Public: the results and the scanned URL appear on the urlscan.io front page and in public search - anyone can see them.
Do not use it for addresses that contain personal data or tokens.
urlscan.full_pending: urlscan.io does not return this scan any more (or it is still running).
usr.copy_title: Copies the address in a defanged form (hxxp, [.])
usr.note_unknown: urlscan.io has no verdict for this page yet. That does not mean it is safe.
usr.note_low: No malicious signals in the urlscan.io data. That is not a guarantee - a fresh phishing page often has no verdict yet.
usr.cert_new_title: A certificate issued in the last week is typical for freshly set up phishing sites
usr.shot_caption:
Screenshot rendered by urlscan.io, click to enlarge
Your browser did not visit the scanned page.
usr.thumb_caption: Thumbnail saved with the scan. Click to enlarge.
usr.shot_missing: urlscan.io has no screenshot for this scan.
usr.legend.score: urlscan.io's own rating of the page: from -100 (likely legitimate) to 100 (likely malicious).
usr.legend_more.score:
A higher score means a stronger suspicion that the page is malicious. Seisa marks a score from 25 as medium and from 60 as high risk.
It is a different number from Seisa's own score in the IP tab: the two measure different things, so they cannot be compared directly.
usr.legend.verdict: urlscan.io's overall call: malicious, suspicious, or no verdict at all.
usr.legend_more.verdict: No verdict does NOT mean 'safe' - it only means urlscan.io has not classified this page either way yet, for example because it is too new or too obscure.
usr.legend.engines_community: Two different sources of opinion about the page.
usr.legend_more.engines_community:
Engines are automatic ratings from outside services (block lists, scanners) - fast, but sometimes wrong. urlscan.io says this field is no longer maintained, so it is often empty.
Community is the votes of registered urlscan.io users who rated the page themselves.
The two can disagree.
usr.legend.categories_brands: A category is the kind of threat (for example phishing, malware).
usr.legend_more.categories_brands: A brand is the company or service the page is impersonating - most often a fake login page pretending to be a bank or a well-known mail provider.
usr.legend.flagged: While a page loads, the browser often connects to many other addresses in the background (images, scripts, ads).
usr.legend_more.flagged: Flagged requests are the ones that went to an address already known to be malicious - meaning the page quietly, without asking, talked to something dangerous.
usr.legend.cert: How many days ago the page's HTTPS certificate, its 'ID card' in the browser, was issued.
usr.legend_more.cert:
A very young certificate (under 7 days) can be a sign of a fresh phishing page: scammers register a new domain and mint a certificate for it right away.
On its own it proves nothing - many honest sites renew their certificate automatically every few weeks, so theirs is young too.
usr.legend.umbrella: The position of this page's host name in Cisco Umbrella's popularity ranking - how often people look it up in DNS.
usr.legend_more.umbrella:
The lower the number, the more popular the name - rank 100 is far better known than rank 900,000.
Popularity is no guarantee of safety: scammers often put their pages on well-known platforms.
usr.legend.apex: The apex domain is the main, registered name (for example example.com), while a subdomain extends it (for example login.example.com).
usr.legend_more.apex: A phishing page often uses a subdomain with a trust-inspiring word (login, secure) tacked onto an apex domain that has nothing to do with the brand it impersonates.
usr.legend.forms: Seisa checks the forms on the page, because fake login pages give themselves away by where they send the password.
usr.legend_more.forms:
The warning sign is a form with a password field that submits its data to a different domain than the page it is on, or submits it unencrypted (plain HTTP instead of HTTPS).
This is a classic sign of credential phishing, so such a form lifts the page's rating to at least medium.
usr.legend.visibility: Who else can see this scan's result on urlscan.io.
usr.legend_more.visibility: public: everyone, including urlscan.io's own search; unlisted: the scan is not shown publicly, but verified security researchers in urlscan Pro can see it; private: only you.
usr.f.title: Page title
usr.f.cert_age: Age on the day of the scan
usr.clipped: Showing the first {shown} of {total}; the rest is in the full API response.
urlscan.existing_need_url: Enter a URL to see the earlier scans of its domain.
urlscan.existing_none: urlscan.io has no earlier scans of this domain.
urlscan.existing_note: The list contains public scans by anyone plus the scans of your urlscan.io account, newest first. Open one instead of ordering a new scan when it is recent enough.
usr.b_form: a password form posts to another domain or over plain HTTP
usr.note_form: urlscan.io has no strong verdict, but the page has a password form posting elsewhere - Seisa rates it at least Medium.
usr.d_forms: Forms found in the rendered page (only the structure is read, nothing from the page is loaded). A password field that posts to another domain is a typical phishing kit.
em.f.scan_title: Put this address into the URLScan tab (nothing is opened or scanned until you click Scan there)

md.service.otx: Number and names of threat-intel pulses linked to this indicator, geolocation, ASN.
md.service.cloudflare: Network/context data - ASN, location, routing. This is not a reputation verdict.
md.service.abuseipdb: Abuse confidence score, number of reports, author of the latest report, ISP, usage type.

dmarc.subtitle: Upload aggregate DMARC reports from mail providers to see which servers send messages on behalf of your domain, whether they pass SPF/DKIM and their alignment, and which IP addresses look suspicious.
dmarc.drop_multiple: You can upload several reports at once; .xml, .gz and .zip files are accepted
dmarc.no_auth_data: no auth_results/{section} data in this record
dmarc.no_records: No records to display in the selected files.
dmarc.banner_bad_one: {n} source fails both SPF and DKIM ({messages}).
dmarc.banner_bad_other: {n} sources fail both SPF and DKIM ({messages}).
dmarc.banner_bad_hint: Check whether these are legitimate senders missing from your SPF/DKIM setup or someone spoofing your domain.
dmarc.banner_warn_one: {n} source fails SPF or DKIM on some messages - DMARC can still pass through the other method.
dmarc.banner_warn_other: {n} sources fail SPF or DKIM on some messages - DMARC can still pass through the other method.
dmarc.banner_good: All sources pass both SPF and DKIM.
dmarc.legend_dmarc: DMARC (Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting and Conformance) is the domain owner's rule that ties SPF and DKIM together: a message is fine if at least one of them passed for the domain in the From field.
dmarc.legend_more_dmarc:
DMARC reports are usually daily summaries from large mailbox providers (for example Google, Microsoft): which servers sent mail on behalf of your domain and whether it passed SPF, DKIM and DMARC.
This tab reads those reports (XML files) and shows which sources are fine and which are not.
dmarc.known_sender: Probably a known sender: {name} (the rDNS name is confirmed by a forward DNS lookup).
dmarc.known_sender_fix: If this is your service, fix its SPF/DKIM setup instead of blocking the address.
dmarc.h_fix: What to fix if this is a legitimate sender
dmarc.fix_dkim_missing: DKIM: the report has no signature. Enable DKIM signing with a key of your domain at this sender.
dmarc.fix_dkim_fail: DKIM: the signature of {domain} (selector {selector}) failed verification. Check that the public key in DNS ({selector}._domainkey.{domain}) is current.
dmarc.fix_dkim_misaligned: DKIM: the signature passes, but for {domain}, which differs from the From header domain ({from}), so it is not aligned. Make the sender sign with your own domain.
dmarc.fix_spf_missing: SPF: the report has no result. Check that the envelope (Return-Path) domain has an SPF record.
dmarc.fix_spf_fail: SPF: the address {ip} is not allowed by the SPF record of {domain}. If this is a legitimate sender, add it to the record (preferably through the service's include:).
dmarc.fix_spf_misaligned: SPF: passes for {domain}, which differs from the From header domain ({from}), so it is not aligned. Make the sender use your own domain as Return-Path or rely on DKIM.
dmarc.timeline_legend: A bar is the number of messages that day (tallest: {max}); the red part is the messages that failed DMARC.
dmarc.legend_spf: SPF (Sender Policy Framework) is a list of servers allowed to send mail on behalf of a domain - like a roster of couriers authorised to deliver on someone else's behalf.
dmarc.legend_more_spf:
This row says whether the server that actually sent the message is on that list.
The raw result (pass/fail/softfail/neutral/none/temperror/permerror) is SPF's own answer, checked against the address in the message's technical 'envelope' (Return-Path, or the server name from HELO when the envelope is empty), not the visible From field.
For SPF to count towards DMARC, the domain it checked also has to match the domain shown in From (this is called alignment) - that is what the second result on this row tells you.
dmarc.legend_dkim: DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail) is a digital signature the sending server adds to the message - like a wax seal proving the content was not altered in transit and that a specific domain (shown as d=, together with a key id s=) signed it.
dmarc.legend_more_dkim: The first result says whether the signature itself is valid; the second says whether the signing domain matches the visible From domain (the same alignment as with SPF) - which is required for DKIM to count towards DMARC.
dmarc.legend_policy: The domain owner sets in their DMARC record (the p= tag) what recipients should do with mail that fails DMARC: nothing (none - just report it), send it to spam (quarantine), or reject it outright (reject).
dmarc.legend_more_policy:
sp is the same choice set separately for subdomains, and np for subdomains that do not exist at all.
pct is an older tag: what percentage of mail the policy applies to. The new version of the standard (RFC 9989) replaced it with the t tag (test mode), but many reports still show pct.
adkim/aspf control how strict alignment has to be (relaxed allows a subdomain of the same domain, strict requires an exact match), and fo controls failure-report options.
A message 'passes' DMARC if either SPF or DKIM passes and is aligned - only one of the two is required.
The 'Decision' column shows what the recipient actually did, which can differ from the stated policy if they made their own exception, for example for mail that was forwarded.
dmarc.err_no_unpack: this browser cannot unpack archives - unpack the file and load the .xml
dmarc.err_too_large: the unpacked report is too large
dmarc.err_archive: the archive could not be read
dmarc.hint_none_ready: {domain}: p=none only monitors, and every source in these reports passes - the policy can likely be tightened to quarantine, then reject.
dmarc.hint_none_risky: {domain}: p=none only monitors, so messages from suspicious sources are delivered untouched. Fix legitimate senders first, then tighten the policy.
dmarc.hint_quarantine_ready: {domain}: p=quarantine and every source in these reports passes - the policy can likely be tightened to reject.
dmarc.hint_pct: {domain}: pct={pct} - the policy applies to only {pct}% of failing messages, the rest is handled with a milder action.
dmarc.legend_table: The SPF and DKIM counts in the table say how many messages passed those checks together with alignment with the From field, not the raw result alone.
dmarc.legend_more_table:
In the DMARC report this is the policy_evaluated field, while the raw SPF and DKIM answers are auth_results.
That is why the same source can look unaligned here even though the raw SPF result said 'pass' - just for a different domain than the one shown in From.
This is very common for forwarded mail, which recipients often mark with their own override, such as forwarded or mailing_list.
dmarc.legend_risk: An assessment of how well-authenticated a message is - not an assessment of whether the sender is malicious.
dmarc.legend_more_risk:
HIGH: at least one message from this address failed DMARC (neither SPF nor DKIM was aligned).
MEDIUM: DMARC always passed, but SPF or DKIM failed for some of the messages.
LOW: every message passed both checks.
The assessment covers one IP address: its worst message counts, not an average.
dmarc.legend_tiles: Suspicious means sources with a high or medium risk (see above).
dmarc.legend_more_tiles:
DMARC-aligned is the percentage of messages where SPF or DKIM passed with alignment.
Policy decisions count messages the recipient actually rejected, quarantined, or delivered unchanged - under a 'none' policy even unaligned mail is still delivered normally, so 'none' does not mean the message was fine.
Override means the recipient made their own exception to the policy (for example because the message had been forwarded).
dmarc.legend_geo: The 'geo' button checks two things at once: where the address block is registered (RDAP, Registration Data Access Protocol: country, owner, network name) and what name that address gives itself in reverse DNS (rDNS - its self-reported 'business card').
dmarc.legend_more_geo:
The 'known sender' label (for example Google, Microsoft 365, Amazon SES) only appears when that rDNS name points back to the very same address - because the rDNS entry itself is set by whoever owns the address block, and could in theory be misleading.
Missing this label does not mean the source is bad, only that it could not be confirmed this way.
dmarc.legend_fix: The hints inside an expanded source follow directly from its own records: a missing DKIM signature, a DKIM signature that fails verification, a signature or SPF record issued for a different domain than the one in From (no alignment), or an address outside the SPF record.
dmarc.legend_more_fix: These hints only make sense for the legitimate sender trying to fix their own setup - if you do not recognise the source, do not 'fix' anything about it; consider reporting it as abuse instead.
dmarc.legend_compare: The comparison matches this import against the previous import of the SAME domain saved in the History tab: which sources are new, which disappeared, which now have a worse risk, and how overall DMARC alignment changed.
dmarc.legend_more_compare: The chart below it shows the number of messages per day (by the report period's start date, in UTC) - the red part of each bar is mail that failed DMARC.
rb.subtitle: Paste the raw source of a suspicious e-mail to prepare and submit an abuse report to AbuseIPDB - with automatic fact extraction, optional AI analysis and full control over the content before sending.
rb.llm_note:
The content is sent to an LLM agent for analysis only after you click "Analyze".
"Analyze without LLM" sends nothing off this computer.
rb.llm_note_warn_text: Always check the proposed report before sending it to AbuseIPDB - it is your responsibility.
rb.attachments_summary: Detected attachments ({n}) - taken into account by the AI in the report comment
rb.llm_full: The model saw the complete message source (headers and the whole body, {chars} characters).
rb.not_qualifying: This e-mail most likely does NOT qualify for a report.
rb.qualifying: The e-mail looks eligible for a report.
rb.llm_failed: The LLM analysis failed ({error}) - showing the rule-based result only.
rb.ai_other_ip: The AI suggests a different IP address than the one detected automatically.
rb.ai_ip_hint: This is only a suggestion - verify it in the chain below and use the button next to the address you want.
rb.check.received_verified: Verified from the Received header (not From/body)
rb.check.not_spoofed_source: The source is trustworthy (established TCP/SMTP connection)
rb.needs_llm: Requires AI analysis - add an OpenRouter key to .env and use "Analyze".
rb.note.received_ok: The address was taken from the Received header.
rb.note.received_other_ip: You chose a different address than the one the program took as the sender. Check in the Received chain that your own receiving server recorded it.
rb.note.received_unsure: The program is not fully sure which Received line was written by your own mail server. Check the Received chain by hand.
rb.note.no_email_auto: No e-mail pasted - cannot be assessed automatically.
rb.note.spoofing_detected: Detected - SPF or DMARC returned fail ({state}). You can select the Spoofing category.
rb.note.spoofing_none: Not detected - the sender passed authentication ({state}). Do not select the Spoofing category.
rb.note.spoofing_nodata: Cannot be assessed - the pasted source has no SPF/DKIM/DMARC results (no Authentication-Results; the receiving server may not have added them, or they were dropped when pasting). Select Spoofing only if you can confirm it another way.
rb.note.spoofing_unclear: Cannot be assessed - the results are ambiguous ({state}). Select Spoofing only if you can confirm it another way.
rb.self_sent_title: Most likely does NOT qualify for a report (local assessment).
rb.self_sent_body: The message looks like a test sent from your own account to yourself ({address}): the sender, the envelope sender and the recipient are the same address, and the headers show no sign of an attack (no SPF/DMARC fail, attachments or ransom demand). No model has read the content - use "Analyze" to confirm.
rb.hard_only_body: Without AI analysis only the hard criteria were checked: a public IP address and an age of up to 60 days. That is not enough to say the e-mail is worth reporting - use "Analyze".
rb.ip_info: AbuseIPDB (90 days): {reports} reports from {users} users, confidence score {score}%, last report {date}.
rb.ip_info_none: AbuseIPDB (90 days): no reports of this address so far.
rb.cooldown: You already reported this address a moment ago. AbuseIPDB accepts the next report of the same IP only after 15 minutes - about {minutes} min left.
rb.prev_reports: You have already reported this address {n} time(s) with Seisa, last on {date}.
rb.llm_blocked: The AI analysis disputed the item above - sending is blocked. Check the Received chain and run "Analyze" again after correcting the data.
em.subtitle:
Paste the full source of an e-mail (headers + body) or load an .eml file.
Seisa breaks it down: first it shows hard facts computed locally - Received route, authentication, domain alignment, timeline, MIME structure, links, hidden content.
In addition, a language model will run a detailed step-by-step analysis, so you learn to read the source of a message.
em.banner:
The whole message with its headers is sent to OpenRouter for analysis after you click "Analyze".
"Analyze without LLM" sends nothing off this computer and shows only the deterministic findings.
Seisa treats the message as untrusted text: it does not open attachments and does not download images or other files the message links to.
em.dup_banner: This message was already analysed on {date} ({details}). Open the saved analysis instead of paying twice, or run the analysis again{more}
em.prep_notes: Preparing the source for the model: {notes}.
em.no_key: No OpenRouter key (OPENROUTER_API_KEY in .env) - showing the deterministic analysis only.
em.model_writing: The model is writing the analysis...
em.aborted: Cancelled - the incomplete analysis was not saved.
em.citations_ok: Citation check (local, free): {n} items checked (IP addresses, quoted headers, SCL/BCL values, identifiers) and all match the source.
em.citations_bad: Citation check: {bad} of {n} checked items do not match the source.
em.citations_hint: This is not always an error (it may be an example, a paraphrase or an abbreviation), but check these places before treating them as true:
em.truncated_banner: The analysis was cut off by the response length limit - its final parts are missing.
em.f.title: Deterministic analysis
em.f.md_intro: Computed locally by Seisa, without a language model. URLs are defanged.
em.f.no_flags: No anomalies were detected automatically (that does not mean there are none).
em.f.received: Message route: Received headers ({n}), from the top (newest)
em.f.received_help: Trust boundary: only the Received header added by the recipient's server is reliable. The roles below are a code heuristic; the final assessment is made by the analysis.
em.f.auth_count: Authentication: SPF / DKIM / DMARC / ARC ({n} result headers)
em.f.auth_help: Only the Authentication-Results written by the recipient's server (authserv-id) counts. A result written by anyone else is just their claim.
em.f.filters: Recipient's anti-spam filters and flags set by the sender

em.facts_show_saved: Show the facts from the day of saving
em.legend.envelope: An e-mail has two sets of addresses, like a letter in an envelope: the envelope is what gets it delivered, the letter is what the reader sees.
em.legend_more.envelope:
The envelope (MAIL FROM and RCPT TO) is the addresses servers use in SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol). The letter is the From, To and Subject headers you see in your mail program. They need not match.
Return-Path is the envelope sender (MAIL FROM) recorded by the recipient's server - bounce notices go back to it. It can differ from From.
Reply-To is the address your reply goes to. SPF, DKIM and DMARC do not check that it matches the sender, so scammers often point it at their own mailbox.
em.legend.received: Every server an e-mail passes through adds a Received header at the top, like a stamp on a parcel, so the route reads from the bottom (the sender) to the top (you).
em.legend_more.received:
Only the entries added by your own mail servers are certain - the lower ones can be written by the sender and can be made up.
An MTA (Mail Transfer Agent) is a server program that passes mail on (for example Postfix, Exim, Exchange). An MUA (Mail User Agent) is a person's mail program (Thunderbird, Outlook, a phone app). An MDA (Mail Delivery Agent) is the last program on the route, which puts the message into the mailbox.
The 'with' field shows the protocol: ESMTP (Extended SMTP) is SMTP with extensions such as STARTTLS encryption or a login, and LMTP (Local Mail Transfer Protocol) is the hand-over to the mailbox store on the operator's side.
HELO (or EHLO) is the name a connecting server announces about itself. It is only a declaration and can say anything.
em.legend.rdns: Reverse DNS (rDNS) is the name attached to an IP address, like a nameplate on a door put up by the owner of the building.
em.legend_more.rdns:
It is stored in a PTR record. The owner of the IP address block sets it, so it is a hint, not proof.
FCrDNS (forward-confirmed reverse DNS) means the PTR name points back to the same IP address. Only then does reverse DNS carry any weight.
em.legend.spf: SPF (Sender Policy Framework) is the list of servers a domain allows to send its mail - like a roster of couriers authorised to deliver on its behalf.
em.legend_more.spf:
The receiver checks whether the IP address of the connecting server is on the list of the envelope domain (MAIL FROM), or of the HELO domain when the envelope is empty.
The envelope domain need not be the one in From, so SPF alone does not protect the visible sender. Only DMARC does that.
em.legend.dkim: DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail) is a digital signature on the message, like a seal on a letter: it shows the content has not changed and which domain signed it.
em.legend_more.dkim:
The signing domain (d=) signs chosen headers and the body, and the receiver checks the signature with the public key published in DNS.
The d= domain need not be the domain in From - that is why DMARC checks whether they match.
em.legend.dmarc: DMARC (Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting and Conformance) is the rule of the From domain's owner that tells receivers how to check whether a message really comes from that domain.
em.legend_more.dmarc:
A message passes DMARC if SPF or DKIM passed for a domain aligned with the From domain - only one of the two is required.
The p= tag says what to do with mail that fails: nothing (none), spam (quarantine) or reject (reject).
em.legend.arc: ARC (Authenticated Received Chain) helps when a message went through an intermediary, such as a forwarder or a mailing list, that breaks SPF or DKIM on the way.
em.legend_more.arc: Each intermediary seals the authentication results it saw. The final receiver can use them, but only if it trusts that intermediary - the seal alone guarantees nothing.
em.legend.authresults: Authentication-Results is the header in which the receiving server writes down the SPF, DKIM and DMARC results - like a note from a border check.
em.legend_more.authresults:
authserv-id is the name of the server that wrote the header (its first word).
Only the header written by your own mail server can be trusted: the sender can add an identical-looking one to fake a good result.
em.legend.tls: TLS (Transport Layer Security) encrypts the connection between two servers, like a sealed envelope on one stretch of the road.
em.legend_more.tls: It protects a single SMTP hop only, not the whole route from the sender to you, and says nothing about whether the sender is legitimate.
em.legend.mime: MIME (Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions) is how an e-mail is split into parts: text, an HTML version and attachments.
em.legend_more.mime: Each part has its own type (Content-Type) and encoding. That is how one message can carry, for example, a photo and a PDF file.
em.legend.messageid: Message-ID is a unique identifier given to the message by the system that sent it - like a parcel's tracking number.
em.legend_more.messageid: The part after the @ is usually the name of the sender's server or software, so it sometimes reveals where the message really came from, despite a different From.
em.legend.scl_bcl: SCL and BCL are ratings from Microsoft's spam filter (Outlook, Microsoft 365) written into the message headers.
em.legend_more.scl_bcl:
SCL (Spam Confidence Level): -1 is a message the filter skipped (for example a trusted sender), 0-1 not spam, 5-6 spam, 8-9 high-confidence spam.
BCL (Bulk Complaint Level, 0-9): how often people complain about a bulk sender (newsletters, for example) - 0 is not bulk mail, 8-9 is a lot of complaints.

lookup.f.name: Name
lookup.compare_trend: Score of the last {n} scans (the outlined bar is this one)
lookup.legend.score: One number from 0 to 100 that combines every source that had something to say about this address or domain.
lookup.legend_more.score:
It is not a plain average: when several sources independently flag the same address as suspicious, the score rises more than a simple average would, while a source with no data at all simply does not affect it.
Below {medium} is low risk, from {medium} up to below {high} is medium, {high} and above is high.
Addresses already known to be safe (AbuseIPDB's allow list, GreyNoise's benign/RIOT tags, OTX-validated) are capped at {cap}, unless some other source reports a strongly contradicting signal.
For a domain (not an IP address), the voters are VirusTotal, OTX and Seisa's own built-in heuristics - AbuseIPDB and GreyNoise only look at IP addresses.
lookup.legend.risk: How dangerous one source on its own thinks this address or domain is, converted by Seisa to a common scale from 0 to 100.
lookup.legend_more.risk:
Seisa turns the source's raw data (for example AbuseIPDB's confidence percentage or the number of VirusTotal engines) into a risk using fixed tables.
That risk enters the combined score with a weight, the source's credibility: from 0.4 for the local heuristics to 0.9 for AbuseIPDB. The weight is below 1 because sources can draw on the same data, so two sources 'agreeing' is not always two independent opinions.
lookup.legend.signal: What Seisa considers worrying enough to show you right away, without clicking anything.
lookup.legend_more.signal:
A source with a risk of {medium} or higher (Medium or High) counts as a signal: its card is at the top of the list, and its jump link in the navigation bar is highlighted in amber.
The other cards hold the same kinds of details - nothing in them concerned the system.
Sources that gave no answer at all (an error, no API key, a used-up quota, or simply not applicable to this kind of address) are grouped into one shared bar at the end of the list.
lookup.legend.identity: Who owns this address or domain - merged into one place from every source that knows something about it.
lookup.legend_more.identity:
For an IP address: its ASN (Autonomous System Number - like the ID number of the courier company that owns this 'street' of addresses), owner, country and network.
The network is the block of IP addresses this address belongs to. Reverse DNS (rDNS) is the name the owner of that block gave this address - a hint, not proof.
For a domain: the registrar, key dates, name servers, IP addresses, mail records, category and popularity.
The badges show how well the sources agree: ✓ all agree, ≈ most agree (click to see what the others say), ⚠ no majority, and '1 source' means only one source knew anything, so there is nothing to compare it against.
The card is open from the start, and its heading says whether the sources agree and names the fields where they differ.
lookup.legend.priority: When sources disagree and there is no clear majority, Seisa still has to pick one value to show as the main one - and it does so by trust, not by chance.
lookup.legend_more.priority:
The official registry (RDAP, Registration Data Access Protocol - the authoritative record of who registered a given block of addresses) wins for owner, network and contact; VirusTotal wins for the ASN; DNS wins over WHOIS for name servers.
This priority never overrides an actual majority vote, and identity never changes the risk score itself.
lookup.legend.country: Two different 'country' fields that can legitimately disagree.
lookup.legend_more.country:
The registration country (from RDAP) is where that block of IP addresses was formally registered - like a courier company's registered head-office address.
The geolocation country is where the address actually appears to be used right now - like the current location of one of that company's vans.
For hosting providers, anycast networks and leased address ranges, these two fields often differ, and that is normal.
lookup.legend.confidence: AbuseIPDB (one of Seisa's sources) collects abuse reports from users worldwide.
lookup.legend_more.confidence:
This number (0-100) is how sure AbuseIPDB is that the address is malicious. What counts most is how many DIFFERENT people reported it and how long ago - old reports weigh less.
That is why it is not a count of reports: a hundred reports from one person mean less than one each from ten people.
Seisa asks AbuseIPDB for the reports from the last 90 days.
lookup.legend.greynoise: GreyNoise recognises addresses that scan the whole internet at once ('background noise'), to tell them apart from an attack aimed at you specifically.
lookup.legend_more.greynoise:
malicious = seen taking part in attacks, benign = a known, harmless scanner or service (for example a search engine indexing pages), unknown = seen, but not rated either way (the default classification).
Background noise alone does not mean someone is attacking you specifically - it is usually just automated scanning of the whole internet.
lookup.legend.riot: GreyNoise's list of well-known business services - CDNs, cloud providers, search engines - essentially a directory of 'loud but legitimate neighbours'.
lookup.legend_more.riot: An address on this list is expected to generate a lot of traffic and is treated as known good.
lookup.legend.pulses: AlienVault OTX collects threat reports from a worldwide community of security researchers - like a network of local outposts reporting suspicious activity.
lookup.legend_more.pulses: Fresh reports with concrete detail (a named threat actor, a malware family, an attack technique) count for more than old, generic bulk lists - and OTX alone never pushes the score up to high by itself.
lookup.legend.whitelisted: AbuseIPDB keeps its own list of addresses it considers safe (large, well-known services, for example).
lookup.legend_more.whitelisted:
If an address is on that list, the risk assigned by this one source is 0 - regardless of what other sources say about the very same address.
AbuseIPDB itself points out that its allow list is generous and should not be the only basis for a decision.
lookup.legend.domain: Two different kinds of information about a domain.
lookup.legend_more.domain:
WHOIS is the registration record - who registered it, when it was created, when it expires, its current status - like an entry in a companies register.
DNS (Domain Name System, the internet's 'address book') is what the domain actually points to today - IP addresses (A/AAAA), name servers, mail servers (MX), security settings (SPF, DMARC, CAA) - like that company's current delivery address.
Name servers (NS) tell the rest of the internet where to look for this domain. MX (Mail Exchange) names the server that receives e-mail sent to this domain.
SPF is the list of servers allowed to send mail on the domain's behalf, DMARC tells recipients what to do with mail that fails DMARC, and CAA (Certification Authority Authorization) restricts which certificate authorities may issue an HTTPS certificate for it.
Wildcard DNS means every possible subdomain resolves, even ones that were never deliberately created.
A dangling NS means the domain points to a name server that no longer exists - whoever registers that server next can take over that part of the domain.
Popularity is the Cloudflare Radar ranking: an exact position only for the top 100 sites worldwide, a bucket (top 200, 500 ...) beyond that.
lookup.legend.heuristics: Weak but free hints computed entirely on your own machine, without sending anything over the network - just from the domain's name and its WHOIS age.
lookup.legend_more.heuristics:
Examples: registered less than 90 days ago, characters that look alike but come from different alphabets (a classic phishing trick), punycode encoding, a top-level domain frequently abused for scams, a label that looks like a random string, or lure words in the name (login, secure ...).
These are only clues, not proof - they can push a domain up to medium risk, but never to high on their own.
lookup.legend.comparison: Only appears when you already scanned this same address or domain before and it is saved in the History tab.
lookup.legend_more.comparison:
It shows: the previous score, the difference from it, the sources whose risk changed by 10 points or more, and one bar per earlier scan (the current one has an outline).
History keeps the last 100 unpinned entries.
rb.payload_title: What will be sent to the API
rb.payload_hint: Exactly what the backend sends to AbuseIPDB: the comment after cleaning (ASCII only, at most 1024 characters), the categories without duplicates and the time in UTC.
rb.hop_internal: An intermediate hop - usually the recipient's or the provider's own infrastructure, not the sender.
rb.check.pii_scan: No personal data in the comment (scan)
rb.legend.groups: Before a report can be sent, Seisa checks several things at once, in three groups of different weight.
rb.legend_more.groups:
Required: the attack age (up to 60 days), the IP address, the category, the gap since the previous report and the verdict. Age, IP address and category are checked by Seisa's code, on the server too, not by the AI.
Blocking: whether the source address from the Received headers is corroborated and not forged. The AI's reading of the e-mail helps here, and any 'no' blocks sending.
Informational checks only warn - you can ignore them and send the report anyway.
rb.legend.boundary_hop: In the chain of 'Received' headers, an e-mail passes through several servers before it reaches you.
rb.legend_more.boundary_hop:
The boundary hop is where the message entered your own mail servers from outside - its IP address is the actual sender.
The entries above it were added by your own servers (for example Gmail or Outlook), while the ones below it were written by the sender's side and can be made up.
rb.legend.smtp_auth: The server recorded that the sender logged into their mail account (SMTP-AUTH), and that account's domain matches the domain of the DKIM signature.
rb.legend_more.smtp_auth:
This corroborates that the message entered the network through exactly this IP address, so the source address is genuine.
It does not mean the sender is honest: the account may have been taken over.
rb.legend.spoofing: Spoofing is pretending a message came from a different domain than it really did - like a letter on someone else's letterhead.
rb.legend_more.spoofing: Seisa flags it when your own mail server recorded that SPF or DMARC failed. That means the domain shown as the sender probably did not send this message.
rb.legend.double_extension: A filename that pretends to be a document but is really a program - for example 'invoice.pdf.exe'.
rb.legend_more.double_extension:
The operating system runs the file according to its LAST extension (.exe), while many people only look at the start of the name and see 'pdf'.
This is a common trick in malicious attachments.
rb.legend.cooldown: AbuseIPDB accepts a report of the same IP address from one account at most once every 15 minutes.
rb.legend_more.cooldown: This is AbuseIPDB's safeguard against duplicate reports flooding its database. Seisa enforces the rule ahead of time, from its own report history, so that sending does not end in an error.
rb.legend.pii: The comment sent to AbuseIPDB is public, so Seisa checks it for personal data before sending.
rb.legend_more.pii: It looks for your own e-mail address, other people's addresses and private IP addresses, and lets you mask them with one click.
rb.legend.confidence: A number from 0 to 100: how sure AbuseIPDB is that this address is malicious.
rb.legend_more.confidence:
What counts most is how many DIFFERENT people reported the address and how long ago - old reports weigh less.
It is NOT a count of reports: a hundred reports from one person mean less than one each from ten people. Seisa asks for the reports from the last 90 days.
rb.legend.qualifies: 'Does this e-mail deserve a report' (yes / no / unknown) is a completely different assessment from the 0-100 risk score in the IP tab.
rb.legend_more.qualifies: An address can have a high risk in the IP tab and still not be eligible for a report here (for example because the attack is too old) - and the other way round.
rb.hint.combine: {name} is meant to accompany a more specific category - add the one that describes the actual attack.
rb.hint.vpn: {name} is a combined category for addresses of VPN services - use it together with the category of the actual abuse.
rb.hint.iot: {name}: name the type of the targeted device in the comment.
rb.hint.spoofing: {name}: the sender passed authentication (SPF or DMARC pass), so the headers do not confirm spoofing.
rb.ip_whitelisted: This address is on the AbuseIPDB whitelist - a report is unlikely to have any effect.
rb.ip_redundant: In the last {days} days this address already has reports in one of the chosen categories (count: {n}) - a new one probably adds only noise. Report it only if you have new facts.
rb.pii_title: The comment may contain personal data
rb.pii_hint:
AbuseIPDB shows comments publicly and is not responsible for personal data you reveal.
Check whether it is your data and mask or remove it before sending.
rb.pii_confirm: The comment still contains {n} item(s) that look like personal data. Send anyway?
rb.sent_score: AbuseIPDB now rates this address at {score}%.
rb.another_ip: Report another address from this e-mail:

rb.cat.1: Tampering with DNS records so that traffic is redirected.
rb.cat.2: Forged data planted in a DNS server's cache.
rb.cat.4: Taking part in a distributed denial-of-service attack.
rb.cat.6: Oversized IP packets sent to crash a target.
rb.cat.9: An open proxy, an open relay or a Tor exit node.
rb.cat.10: Comment or forum spam and other CMS spam.
rb.cat.11: Spam in the message body, infected attachments, phishing e-mails. Keep the comment to relevant facts.
rb.cat.12: Spam comments on blogs and CMS sites.
rb.cat.13: Combined category for addresses of VPN services.
rb.cat.14: Probing for open ports and vulnerable services.
rb.cat.17: Forging the identity of an e-mail sender.
rb.cat.18: Password guessing against websites and services (SSH, FTP, SIP, SMTP, RDP).
rb.cat.19: Scrapers and crawlers that ignore robots.txt or fake their user agent.
rb.cat.20: A host that is probably infected and used to attack others; combine with other categories.
rb.cat.21: Probing or exploiting web applications (CMS, shops, forums, plugins).
rb.cat.22: Abuse of Secure Shell; combine with a more specific category.
rb.cat.23: An attack aimed at an Internet-of-Things device; name the device type in the comment.
